reviewHtml:
Talk about going out with a bang. Glenn Martens ended his six-year story at Diesel this afternoon with a collection containing all the gestures Diesel lovers lust after: disintegration, hybridization, pop, tailored tension, and unstructured release. It powerfully signaled a designer who has plenty left in the tank. Now all that Martens energy will be focused exclusively on Maison Margiela.

Speaking backstage pre-show, Martens championed the team he has built around him since arriving here in 2020. He said: “If you think about it, six years ago it was literally T-shirts and five-pocket trousers, and look at all of it now. I’m so proud of everybody. It’s one of the most amazing things to see all of these butterflies becoming fantastic.” He added that he was leaving Renzo Rosso’s core brand with “a great platform” and a team “ready for a next chapter.” Martens should certainly feel he can ride into Diesel’s sunset with his head held high. Today he wore sunglasses indoors for the first time at one of his shows here.

Martens’s first Vogue Runway–reviewed collection for Diesel, spring 2022, opened with the model Ella Snyder. Today he closed with her too. There were some wonderful pieces of fabric development to support the underlying feel of a slow peeling that permeated this collection: Denim was coated, then lasered to resemble leather; orchid-shaped cutaways appeared to eat into knits and polos; foil-printed surfaces cracked open to reveal trompe l’oeil suggestions of other garments beneath. Elsewhere, T-shirts and sweatshirts were shredded almost to remnants, while tailoring and shirting seemed caught up, twisted, and partially undone, as if half-torn from the body.

The mood this signified was foreplayed by the heavy breathing that ran over the PA before a slowly rising techno mix revealed itself midway through as a beautiful nosebleed variation on Donna Summer’s “Love to Love You Baby.” As the music built and Summer moaned, scores of Diesel-wearing plants in the audience started making out with increasingly enthusiastic abandon. Sex positivity has run through all of Martens’s work at Diesel: After last season’s walk of shame, he was nipping back for a second taste. It was an uproarious scene that had the crowd screaming as Snyder closed the finale and the designer took his final bow.

Martens really came good at Diesel.
